questions.question: Compare rural and urban areas.
questions.expected_answer: Rural areas are the countryside, with farms, villages and open land, fewer people spread out, and many people working in primary activities such as farming, forestry and fishing; they often have fewer services and are quieter. Urban areas are towns and cities, with many people living close together, many buildings and roads, and most people working in secondary activities in factories or tertiary activities in shops, offices, schools and hospitals; they have more services but also problems such as traffic, pollution, crime and overcrowding.

questions.question: Explain urbanisation using push and pull factors.
questions.expected_answer: Urbanisation is the growth in the share of people living in towns and cities, mostly through migration from rural areas. Push factors drive people out of rural areas, such as a lack of jobs, poverty, few services, poor schools, drought and too little land. Pull factors attract people to cities, such as jobs, higher wages, better schools, hospitals, electricity, water and entertainment, and family already living there. In South Africa, urbanisation speeded up after influx control laws were removed in 1986.

questions.question: Describe the results of urbanisation for both cities and rural areas.
questions.expected_answer: In cities, many people find jobs, schools and health care, but fast growth means not enough houses, services and jobs for everyone, so informal settlements grow, sometimes on unsafe land, with traffic, pollution and unemployment. In rural areas, many young adults leave, so villages may have mostly grandparents and children, and fewer people farm, but money sent home helps households. Many people keep links with both places through circular migration.
